chapter: The House That Jazz Built and Homestead childhood
title: Music in the home: the victrola, piano rolls and sheet music
summary: Records and piano rolls such as Fats Waller, song sheets and a victrola in every home.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: Can I ask you a little bit about that? You've probably told us the answer to this question, I think, but I want to ask it again anyway.
Was there a lot of music in the home when you were growing up -- in the homes I guess?

Well, yeah, going back to when I was a baby, around 3 or 4 years old, my grandmother, my father's mother, they had a player piano and my aunt in Ranken, she had a piano and she had the victrola, we called it that, so I heard a lot of music. And just about everybody had the victrolas when they came out.

I recall how we happened to get our victrola was, there was somebody coming around offering me victrolas like a dollar down and a dollar a week and 99 free records. So everybody wound up with a victrola. So there was an awful lot of music going on.
Do you remember some of the music that you heard -- on the piano rolls, for instance, way back?

Some of the earlier piano rolls I heard were some by Fats Waller. I suppose Eubie Blake must have made some piano rolls and I wouldn't pay much attention to the label, as to who made the roll, but I do know that some of the songs were the popular songs of the day. "Avalon," "'Til We Meet Again," some of those early -- and then when the War was imminent, there was music like "The Drafting Blues," and things like that. And of course in the local five and ten -- Woolworth's or McCrory's, they always had a pianist there who would play all the currently popular music and we bought a lot of sheet music then. I can't remember all the songs we got, but we had the sheet music. I would

look at the sheet music to learn the words in the songs. I don't know how many people around there, how many musicians, how many piano players actually read the music, but they read enough to be able to play the tunes. And then they heard them played at the five and ten. I guess a lot of them were playing by ear anyway. It wasn't too difficult to pick up the songs in those days, there wasn't too much to remember.

But then there were song sheets that a local retail store, I remember, when they would have a sale, they would have one of the stores who had a son who sang, and he would come around with a megaphone and sing some of the currently popular tunes to advertise the sale, and we'd get words to songs that way.
But getting back to music in the home, everybody had a victrola, mostly everybody had a piano. So there was always something going on.
There wasn't any one piece of music that had any kind of dramatic impact on you, you know, that made you --
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943

Not really, not really. We got all the latest records as they came out and there was just so much. I don't think I really got interested enough in music to pay attention to who was doing what until I heard a recording by Ethel Waters, and of course we had Mamie Smith's recording of the "Crazy Blues" and we had all of the race records, Ma Rajney (phonetic spelling) and Bessie Smith, Clara Smith and we had recordings by Louie Armstrong and McKinney's Cotton Pickers, and of course one of the early race records, it wasn't considered a race record, but it was just a general record on the Gennett label, the one that Lois Deppe made with Earl Hines and Harry, but I think that Harry probably brought those to Homestead from New York because the band had come to New York. He had worked here. But I think he must have brought those back from New York with him when he came home, that's how we happened to have those.
